rule: adjusted_score desc, total_score desc; dedupe by arXiv id / URL / id / title

papers.title: From Item Scores to Semantic Tokens: Test-Time Collaborative Adaptation for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Xiongfeng Shan, Xing Tang, Hanchong Chen, Fuyuan Lyu, Lingjie Li, Jingyan Jiang, Duguang Liu, Xiuqiang He
papers.summary: In generative recommendation with semantic IDs, the model writes an item's code one token at a time, and beam search keeps only the highest-scoring prefixes at each step. Once a prefix is pruned, every item beneath it can never be generated. The problem is sharpest when a user has just developed a new interest that shows up in only one or two recent interactions. This paper proposes TCBSA (test-time collaborative beam search adaptation), which ==turns a scoring model's item scores into bonuses on code prefixes before every pruning step==. The scoring model scores the whole catalog and keeps the top few hundred items; each item's margin above the cutoff is spread over every step of its code. Before each beam search ranking step, these bonuses are added to the path's cumulative score. Neither model is retrained. Added to TIGER, it raises NDCG@10 by a relative 4.9% to 30.4%, depending on the public dataset. With a narrower beam, it is also more accurate and faster than TIGER with a wider beam.

papers.title: PinRec: Unified Generative Retrieval Model for Pinterest Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Edoardo Botta, Jaewon Yang, Yi-Ping Hsu, Laksh Bhasin, Yilin Chen
papers.summary: Recommender systems usually run a separate retrieval model for the home feed, search and related items, because each surface wants something different: saves on the home feed, outbound clicks to buy on search, and continued browsing on related items. This Pinterest KDD 2026 paper replaces all three with one generative retrieval model, PinRec. It is pretrained on site-wide behavior, fine-tuned on each surface's logs, and told at generation time which action to aim for. ==Conditioning on the target action matters far more than unifying the model==. Removing that condition cuts offline recall on the three surfaces by 7.5% to 12.6%. Added to search as one retrieval source online, it raised saves by 3.88%.

papers.title: CoFiRec: Coarse-to-Fine Tokenization for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Tianxin Wei, Xuying Ning, Xuxing Chen, Ruizhong Qiu, Yupeng Hou
papers.summary: When shopping online, people usually look at a broad category before picking a specific item. Yet most generative recommenders build Semantic IDs by mashing an item's category, title, description and collaborative signal into one vector before quantizing it, so that coarse-to-fine structure is lost. This UIUC and Meta paper proposes CoFiRec, which ==splits an item into category, text and collaborative levels, codes each separately, and generates them coarse to fine==. Across several public datasets and backbones, it beats the strongest traditional and generative baselines by 7.27% on average in Recall and NDCG. On cold items the gain reaches 10.0%, versus 4.7% on warm items.

papers.title: Unifying Behavior Modeling and Semantic Generation for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Binquan Wu, Xinbo Chen, Yicheng Luo, Yuhao Ke, Jingye Li
papers.summary: Generative recommenders that write the next item's Semantic ID code by code have a systematic bias. This KDD 2026 paper from South China University of Technology finds that the fewer items in a user's history share the target's category, the worse they do against classic behavior-only sequential models; in the worst group, TIGER's NDCG@10 trails SASRec by 30%. The cause: the encoder learns which item comes next, while the decoder must write its code. OMG inserts a two-layer network between them; each step adds the previous state to the encoder's final state and runs it through the network again. ==Each step predicts both the next item and the first code, with the latter weighted more each step==, and all intermediate states go to the decoder. That one part lifts metrics by 14.5% on average while adding only 0.16% compute.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation across Item and Code Spaces for Parallel Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Yixuan Xu, Hailin Liu, Linxiang Peng, Can Yang
papers.summary: In generative recommendation with Semantic IDs, training only tells the model which item came next, so it learns nothing about how likely the other items were given the same history. A classic sequential recommender can provide that distribution, but it scores items while the generative model predicts codes position by position, so the knowledge is hard to distill directly. This paper from HKUST and others proposes two distillation objectives for parallel models that predict all code positions at once. One rebuilds a catalogue-wide item distribution from the student's code predictions and aligns it with the teacher; ==the other spreads the teacher's item probabilities onto each code position==. On average, the first lifts Recall@10 by 15.39% and the second lifts NDCG@10 by 8.28%.

papers.title: Separating Thinking from Spelling for Efficient Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Danil Gusak, Anna Volodkevich, Ivan Oseledets, Evgeny Frolov
papers.summary: Generative recommenders retrieve by writing an item's Semantic ID code by code, and every beam-search step runs through the large backbone, so the cost grows with more candidates and longer codes. It is often the main expense. This paper proposes Deco, which separates reading the history from writing the code. The backbone reads the history once and condenses it into a vector for the next item, and ==a light cached decoder runs the whole beam search==, with codes and the prefix tree unchanged. On seven e-commerce, movie and music datasets, accuracy matches or beats the original model. Under a 50 ms latency budget, throughput is 3.2 to 8.6 times higher.

papers.title: SAGE: Sequence-level Adaptive Gradient Evolution for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Yu Xie, Xing Kai Ren, Ying Qi, Ping Yang, Yao Hu
papers.summary: Generative recommenders are often trained with supervision first, then aligned to user feedback on whole slates with reinforcement learning. To keep training stable, each update may change the probability of generating a slate only by a fixed ratio set per sample, which smothers rare positive feedback on cold items and barely punishes repetitive negative slates. This Xiaohongshu paper proposes SAGE, which only changes the optimizer: ==positive slates get a higher cap on how far their probability can rise==. Repetitiveness is measured by the entropy of the slate's item categories, and the further a negative slate's entropy falls below its recent average, the further its probability may be pushed down. On Amazon data, top-K accuracy holds while offline cold-start recall rises by about 90% to 101% and diversity by about 11%.

papers.title: TGR-EvoDAG: A DAG-based Multi-Agent Code Evolution Framework for Generative Recommendation on Tencent
papers.authors: Junlin He, Junzhang Zhu, Yudong Li, Yihong Tang, Xuefeng Jiang, Wei Ma, Chengxiang Zhuo, Zang Li
papers.summary: Letting LLM agents rewrite code to search for better recommenders runs into two problems in generative recommendation. Retraining the tokenization, pretraining and alignment stages costs very different amounts, yet agents spend budget as if it were uniform. And a good upstream change often makes metrics worse until downstream stages adapt, so it gets discarded too early. This Tencent paper proposes TGR-EvoDAG, which ==keeps several improvement branches alive in a directed acyclic graph==. Each node is an edited version of the code that records which pipeline stages the edit touched and its retraining GPU hours. Upstream edits that first hurt metrics are kept until downstream edits adapt, then the branches are merged, and budget goes by expected gain versus retraining cost. On Tencent's commercial media platform, the evolved model raised online click-through rate by a statistically significant 0.40%.

papers.title: GUIDER: Generative User Interest Discovery via Explicit Reasoning with Large Language Models
papers.authors: Jinke Wu, Yinghao Wu, Shuchang Liu, Yandong Bai, Qi Zhu
papers.summary: The Semantic IDs common in generative recommendation are opaque strings of codes: it is hard to see what the model generated or why, and the LLM's own reasoning goes unused. GUIDER splits recommendation into two steps. ==The LLM first reasons in text about which interest circles the user may want next==. Circles are interest topics described in words and must come from a fixed set; items are then matched within the chosen topics. In reinforcement learning, invented circles outside the set lose reward, and so does overlong thinking. Large-scale online A/B tests on Kuaishou show steady gains in average app time and more exploration beyond users' existing interests.

papers.title: MPQ: A Message-Passing View of Post-Training Quantization
papers.authors: Yanshuo Chen, Chenxi Liu, Reza Shirkavand, Heng Huang
papers.summary: When an LLM is quantized after training to very low bit widths, common solvers such as GPTQ decide block by block which codebook value each group of weights takes. Once a block is fixed it never changes, and near-tied alternatives are dropped. This paper proposes MPQ (message-passing quantization), which ==keeps probabilities over each block's candidate values and commits only at the end==. It alternates between two steps. One uses the layer's output error to estimate each block's weights as continuous values along with how reliable that estimate is. The other gives each candidate a probability: candidates closer to the estimate score higher, and the less reliable the estimate, the more even the probabilities. After a few rounds each block takes its most probable value, and blockwise coordinate descent polishes the result. On Llama, Qwen and Mistral models it improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, with larger gains at lower bit widths. With Llama-3-8B at 2 bits, its perplexity is about 11.6, against 12.76 for the baseline.

papers.title: Hierarchical GTV Estimation: Bridging the Gap between Container-Level Ranking and Item-Level Conversion
papers.authors: Zerong Lan, Fan Zhang, Chuang Chen, Tianchun Huang, Teng Zhang, Xingxing Wang
papers.summary: Local-services and live-commerce ads are ranked and billed per store or livestream room, but users actually buy one voucher or one product inside it, so directly predicting how much a click will sell gives a noisy label that is hard to learn. This Meituan paper splits a store's expected sales into parts: first whether the user orders at all, then each voucher's purchase probability and quantity, multiplied by its price and summed. A store-level regression tower covers samples whose voucher-level signal is too sparse. ==Each sub-task gets a far more stable label==. In a 13-day online A/B test, ad revenue per search rose 1.42%, and the method is fully deployed.

papers.title: iFusion: Integrating Dynamic Interest Streams via Diffusion Model for Click-Through Rate Prediction
papers.authors: Ziheng Ni, Congcong Liu, Yuying Chen, Zhiwei Fang, Changping Peng, Zhangang Lin, Ching Law, Jingping Shao
papers.summary: CTR models usually encode long-term and short-term behavior separately, then concatenate or gate them into one interest vector, so one-off noise in recent behavior, such as stocking up during a sale or buying for someone else, gets written straight into long-term preference. This JD.com ICLR 2026 paper treats long-term interest as a draft: it adds noise, then denoises step by step conditioned on the latest sessions to produce the fused interest vector. ==Each session splits in two: averaging keeps repeated preferences, attention catches sudden interests==, and the stable path gets about twice the weight. In a 7-day online A/B test, CTR rose 2.44% while serving latency grew only about 0.3%.

papers.title: MARS: Multi-resolution Adaptive Routing for Sequential Recommendation
papers.authors: Ming Yin, Sixun Dong, Yudong Liu, Wen-Yun Yang, Yunjiang Jiang, Yiran Chen
papers.summary: To save compute, long-history recommenders compress a user's thousands of actions into a small set of cached vectors. This Duke and Meta paper finds that such caches barely remember a user's latest actions while very old ones survive best: ==recent interests get buried under old ones==. MARS writes the history into four memory tracks at once. With each new action, every track fades old content at its own rate: one halves it within a few actions, another only after hundreds. When reading, a small router scores the tracks and each cached vector reads only the top two. On KuaiRec, AUC rises from 0.793 to 0.804, with about 2% more scoring latency.

papers.title: Adaptive Diffusion-based Augmentation for Recommendation
papers.authors: Na Li, Fanghui Sun, Yan Zou, Yangfu Zhu, Xiatian Zhu
papers.summary: Recommenders train on negatives drawn from items a user never clicked. Random picks teach little, while picking the items the model scores highest often turns things the user would like but never saw into false negatives. This AAAI 2026 paper from Harbin Institute of Technology and others synthesizes negatives with a diffusion model: it noises a liked item's vector step by step, learns to restore it, and takes a half-restored vector as the negative. Which step is used depends on the model's score for the item: a higher score means it takes more noise to become unrecognizable, so a noisier step is chosen. ==A synthetic negative matches no real item, so it never penalizes what the user wants==. On weaker models such as NGCF, Recall@10 rises by up to 69%; on MixGCF and others that already mine hard negatives, the gain is only 1% to 5%.

papers.title: GCIB: Graph Contrastive Information Bottleneck for Multi-Behavior Recommendation
papers.authors: Likang Wu, Zihao Chen, Jianxin Zhang, Sangqi Zhu, Yuanyuan Ge, Haipeng Yang, Lei Zhang
papers.summary: Multi-behavior recommenders use auxiliary behaviors such as views, favorites and add-to-cart to make up for sparse target behavior like purchases, but many auxiliary interactions have nothing to do with the target and pull user and item embeddings off course. GCIB works on two levels. On the graph, it learns to drop edges from the auxiliary graph so that what remains reflects the target-behavior graph while carrying as little else from the original as possible; the dropped edges are mostly irrelevant interactions. On features, it contrasts the denoised auxiliary features with the target features as two views. ==Auxiliary behavior fills gaps without being taken wholesale==. The paper reports beating existing methods on several real-world datasets.

papers.title: Beyond Single Embedding: Modeling User Preferences as Distribution in Federated Recommendation
papers.authors: Chunxu Zhang, Weipeng Zhang, Guodong Long, Zhiheng Xue, Bo Yang
papers.summary: In federated recommendation each device sees only a fragment of a user's behavior, yet most methods still represent a user with one fixed embedding, as if preferences were settled and precisely knowable. With little data, that estimate is brittle. This paper represents a user's preference as a distribution instead: a diffusion model generates several preference vectors that all fit the user's observed behavior, and the user is represented by that set rather than a single point. ==Evidence is not squeezed into a single point too early==. On federated recommendation benchmarks, the paper reports steadier rankings, more robustness under ambiguous feedback, and consistent gains over baselines.

papers.title: SynRec: Synergistic multi-domain recommendation with frequency-guided expert specialization
papers.authors: ['Zechuan Wang', 'Dong Wang', 'Ming Zong', 'Guogang Cao']
papers.summary: When several businesses each run their own recommender and share no users, knowledge cannot be transferred between them through shared user IDs. This paper proposes SynRec, which lets several domains share one Transformer recommender and ==shares only domain-agnostic behavior patterns, such as the fast and slow rhythms of behavior sequences over time==. It replaces the feed-forward layer with a domain-aware mixture of experts (MoE): some experts serve all domains and learn shared patterns, while others serve only one domain and learn its differences, which limits domains dragging each other down. Across 6 domains with no shared users, it beats the single-domain models in every domain and is the best of the evaluated multi-domain methods in 5 of them.

papers.title: Bayesian Ensemble for Sequential Decision-Making
papers.authors: Rui Liu, Enmin Zhao, Lu Wang, Yu Li, Ming Pang, Changping Peng, Zhangang Lin, Ching Law, Jingping Shao
papers.summary: Recommendation and reinforcement learning often use an ensemble to estimate uncertainty: each decision samples one member, and disagreement among members signals uncertainty. The sampling is usually fixed and uniform, regardless of which member has been doing well. This paper proposes Bayesian Ensemble (BE), which ==treats choosing a member as a bandit problem of its own==: it updates each member's selection probability by Bayesian inference on the rewards it observes. BE is a thin layer on top of existing ensembles. The authors attach it to bandit learning and to DQN, and report better results and good efficiency in both synthetic and real-world environments.

papers.title: Bridging Exploration and Persona: Information-Directed Dueling for Test-Time Agent Personalization
papers.authors: Jie Mao, Pingchen Lu, Xiangyi Wang, Hengquan Huang, Shuang Qiu, Min Zhang, Zhongxiang Dai
papers.summary: The same user may want a bold collaborator when brainstorming with an AI assistant and a strict critic when editing, so one fixed persona rarely fits. This paper lets the assistant switch personas from light feedback: the user simply prefers one of two answers, and the assistant picks the best of several hundred pre-built personas. Each round, the current top persona defends its spot against a challenger. A neural model estimates how far each candidate trails the champion, a light statistical model estimates how much one comparison would cut uncertainty about the ranking, and the candidate with the best ratio of the two is chosen. ==A new query starts from the win-loss records of similar earlier queries==. Tested on seven personalized generation benchmarks with ten comparisons per query and two simulated judges per benchmark, it ranks first in 13 of those 14 results.

papers.title: Semantically Rich, Metrically Affect-Blind: A Geometric Blind Spot in Modern Text Embedders
papers.authors: Mahdi Naser Moghadasi
papers.summary: Search a vector index for what users dislike about a product, and the reviews you get back are usually on topic but a mix of praise and complaints. This paper measures why. Across 11 text embedding models, sentiment is present in the vectors and a simple linear classifier can read it, yet the cosine similarity that retrieval actually uses barely registers it. ==A small projection head on the frozen embedder, trained in seconds on a CPU, repairs this==. It is trained contrastively on a few thousand sentiment-labeled sentences, pulling same-sentiment sentences together and pushing opposite ones apart. When a review sentence is used to find similar sentences, more of those with the same sentiment rank near the top, and the MAP measuring this rises by up to 26 points. The cost is a lower score on the general semantic similarity benchmark STS-B, but after concatenating the head's output with the original vector, it is only 2.4 to 12 points below the original vector.

papers.title: LightRetriever: A LLM-based Text Retrieval Architecture with Extremely Faster Query Inference
papers.authors: Guangyuan Ma, Yongliang Ma, Xuanrui Gou, Zhenpeng Su, Ming Zhou, Songlin Hu
papers.summary: In LLM-based text retrieval, documents can be encoded offline, but queries arrive in real time, so every query runs the full LLM, which keeps throughput low and serving costly. LightRetriever breaks the symmetry: documents still go through the full LLM, while the query side is reduced to a table lookup. During training, a shared prompt plus a single token is fed through the LLM to get that token's vector, and a query vector is the average of its token vectors. ==Every vocabulary token's vector can be precomputed into one table==, so at serving time a query is just lookups and an average. Versus running a full LLM on an A800 GPU, query encoding is over 1000 times faster and end-to-end retrieval throughput rises more than tenfold, while keeping about 95% of the full LLM retriever's retrieval scores on average across benchmarks.

papers.title: System One models Are Not Better Rerankers
papers.authors: Michael Dinzinger, Kanishka Ghosh Dastidar, Michael Granitzer
papers.summary: Using the new decision models to rerank search results does not beat a purpose-tuned reranker, concludes this University of Passau paper. Decision models, also called System One models, answer a question with a calibrated probability of yes instead of text, and within weeks of release they were used for reranking. The paper compares two fine-tunes of the same backbone: decision fine-tuning trains on all kinds of yes-or-no questions to give accurate probabilities, while reranker fine-tuning trains only on MS MARCO queries and passages to judge relevance. Across six Qwen backbones of different sizes and ten TREC DL and BEIR collections, ==reranker fine-tuning wins on every small and mid-sized backbone==, by 5 to 29 points nDCG@10 up to 9B, and the two tie at 27B. Below that size, decision fine-tuning is no better than asking the untuned model. The authors' advice is blunt: if you need a reranker, fine-tune a reranker.

papers.title: PersonalQuery-Benchmark:Evaluating Retrieval Robustness to Personalized User Expression Differences
papers.authors: Wenyu Liang, Hongzhi Yin, Tongtong Wu, Fan Liu, Kexin Dai, Weiqing Wang
papers.summary: Two shoppers want the same product. One asks for strawberry, lactose-free Greek yogurt in a short phrase; the other writes a longer sentence and misspells a word along the way. Will search return the same results? This paper builds a benchmark, PQB, from real user reviews in three Amazon categories to test whether results hold up when the same need is worded differently. They often do not. With the core product terms identical and only sentence structure changed, among query pairs where one query puts the target product first, roughly 27% to 52% of the time the other does not. Misspellings that follow the user's own typing habits cut the top-20 hit rate by up to 12.3 percentage points. ==Models with better overall effectiveness are not necessarily more robust==.

papers.title: What the Query Remembers: Query Abstraction Governs Lexical and Dense Retrieval of Classical Arabic Poetry
papers.authors: Omar Farouk Zouak, Selma Mani, Larbi Said Chikh, Raid Abderrezak Ouahioune
papers.summary: When searching a classical Arabic poetry archive, which works better: keyword search with BM25 or an embedding model? This paper finds that the answer depends mainly on how much of the original wording the user still remembers. When users half-remember a few lines, BM25 beats all nine embedding models. When users can only describe what the poem is about, BM25 drops to 8th of 10 systems. ==By rewriting the same queries, the authors show that the ranking is driven by whether the query contains original wording==. Adding half a verse of the original to a query raises BM25 recall by 37.8 points.

papers.title: Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations
papers.authors: Shubham Gupta, Siva Reddy, Perouz Taslakian, Valentina Zantedeschi, Cem Subakan
papers.summary: In contrastive models like CLIP and CLAP, the two modalities are trained to align yet their embeddings often sit in offset regions, a phenomenon called the modality gap. This paper leaves the backbone untouched and changes only the space the embeddings live in: the unit sphere is replaced by the probability simplex, where every dimension is nonnegative and all dimensions sum to one. In practice a light softmax adapter is attached to each output, and similarity is computed as total variation distance between the two distributions. ==Both modalities are forced into the same coordinate system, and the offset nearly vanishes==. On five cross-modal retrieval benchmarks, the distance between the modality centroids shrinks by 97% to 99%, with retrieval matching or beating standard models.

papers.title: MICE to Meet You: From Re-ranking Only to End-to-End Retrieval
papers.authors: Victor Morand, Yuxuan Zong, Mathias Vast, Josiane Mothe, Benjamin Piwowarski
papers.summary: Cross-encoders rerank candidate documents most accurately, but every candidate must be fully processed for every query. This paper gives the faster MICE architecture a document storage scheme, MICE-P, which comes close to cross-encoder ranking quality at about a quarter of the per-query time. In MICE, the first layers encode the query and the document separately, so the document part can be precomputed; the later layers let query tokens attend to the stored document token representations. MICE-P compresses each document token vector to 128 dimensions, ==stores it in PLAID format, and decompresses it at query time==. PLAID clusters token vectors into centroids and stores each vector as its nearest centroid's ID plus a quantized residual. On BEIR public datasets, its average nDCG@10 is only 0.9 points below a cross-encoder of similar size.

papers.title: 56 scanned pages to a cited answer in 5 minutes: RAG pipeline for the documents search cannot read
papers.summary: Much enterprise knowledge sits in scanned PDFs that ordinary search cannot read. This Elastic tutorial builds a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline: upload a scanned 56-page plant guide, ask in plain language, and within minutes get an answer citing the page it came from. The key piece is jina-ocr-v1, which reads one page image per pass and outputs Markdown in reading order, keeping tables as tables, transcribing handwriting and dropping headers and footers. ==Parsed pages are chunked and embedded automatically at ingest, then searched with hybrid keyword and semantic retrieval==, and an LLM writes the cited answer. The whole pipeline runs on one platform with no model or GPU deployment.

papers.title: Beyond Post-Hoc Rewards: Privileged Reasoning Exploration for Multimodal Embeddings
papers.authors: Tianyu Yang, Yijun Tian, Lars Benedikt Kaesberg, Jan Philip Wahle, Bela Gipp, Terry Ruas, Daniel Kurzawe
papers.summary: Some multimodal embedding models first have the model write reasoning about the input and then embed it along with the input, producing richer vectors. But training data only says which pairs are relevant, never what reasoning to write, so exploring from the input alone rarely finds reasoning that actually helps retrieval. PILOT has one multimodal LLM play two roles: one writes reasoning from the input only, while the other also sees the matching target during training and so finds useful reasoning more easily. ==Some of the second role's reasoning is transferred to the first==, weighted by two things: how well the embedding built with that reasoning retrieves, and how likely the first role would be to write it from the input alone. Only the first is used at inference. On the 78-task MMEB-V2, overall scores rise by 3.2 and 3.3 points at 2B and 7B, with the largest gains in visual-document retrieval.

papers.title: Collection-Date Assignment Redirects Answers in Temporal QA
papers.authors: Minsu Oh, Seunghui Jwa, Soo Kyun Kim, Yeo-Chan Yoon
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented question-answering systems often attach a collection date to web snippets, and this paper finds that ==this field, which only records the fetch day, can steer an LLM's answer the wrong way==, even though it says nothing about when the content changed. Ask which team an ice hockey player played for on a given day, and put both an older and a newer Wikipedia revision in the context. The texts and revision timestamps stay fixed; only the collection dates are swapped, so the older revision's date equals the question date. The experiment covers 595 Wikipedia pages. The swap lowers five open-weight models' exact-match rate on the newer answer by 37.6 to 51.4 percentage points, and telling the model not to choose by collection time barely reduces the loss.

papers.title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Yijing Ke, Tianle Cai, Ruosong Wang
papers.summary: LLM reinforcement learning usually generates answers with one inference engine and trains with another framework. Even with identical weights and BF16 on both sides, the numbers differ slightly, so an update meant to be on-policy quietly becomes off-policy and training can suddenly collapse. This paper from ByteDance Seed and Peking University finds that the two systems need not be aligned wholesale. It is enough to round at the same place on both sides in three spots, RoPE, SwiGLU and residual RMSNorm, keeping those intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. ==With all three aligned, four Qwen-family models no longer collapse==, and aligning RoPE alone also suffices. The inference engine, matmul and attention kernels, and the training objective stay unchanged.

papers.title: KVStream: Adaptive Parallel Storage Management for KV Caching in Large-Scale LLM Serving
papers.authors: Avinash Maurya, Jaiaid Mobin, Jie Ye, M. Mustafa Rafique, Franck Cappello, Bogdan Nicolae
papers.summary: Long-context inference keeps reusing the same prefixes: system prompts, whole documents, code repositories and multi-turn session histories. Their KV cache no longer fits in GPU memory or host memory, so it has to live on disk and be read back on the next hit, which puts disk reads on the critical path of every inference step. Existing systems read only from the node-local NVMe, while the parallel file system that every cluster already mounts sits almost idle. This paper builds KVStream: every KV chunk is written to both the local disk and the shared storage. ==At read time both tiers read at once, and whichever finishes first claims the next batch==. Plugged into LMCache, it reaches up to 1.49x LMCache's offline throughput and up to 6.1x lower mean TTFT under bursty traffic.

papers.title: C 2 KV: Compressed and Composable KV Cache Reuse for Efficient LLM Inference
papers.authors: Chuheng Du, Junyi Chen, Hanlin Tang, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation stitches several retrieved documents into the context, and recomputing their KV caches from scratch every time is expensive, so some methods store each document's KV cache and concatenate them on use. But long documents have huge KV caches, so storing and loading them becomes the bottleneck, and naively compressing them before concatenation hurts accuracy badly. This paper from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Alibaba proposes C2KV: a light extractor beside the frozen model reads each document followed by a few learnable compression tokens and keeps only those tokens' KV as the document's cache. ==Caches are stored without positions, which are re-applied at concatenation time==, so they combine like building blocks. On long contexts, inference is up to 17 times faster with generation quality largely preserved.

papers.title: Advancing Generative Recommendation Inference: our collaboration with NVIDIA on TensorRT LLM
papers.summary: By moving generative podcast recommendation off two separate inference engines and onto TensorRT-LLM together with NVIDIA, Spotify cut beam search cost by up to 54% and scoring cost by up to 7% on Qwen3-1.7B. Spotify recommends with semantic IDs, and a single online request needs three kinds of inference: beam search to generate candidates, scoring a given batch of candidates, and inserting the user vector into the prompt as one extra token. These used to be split across two inference engines, vLLM and SGLang, and vLLM's beam search could not saturate the GPU, so Spotify fell back to lower-tier cards. The two companies added the missing features to TensorRT-LLM and ==unified all three in one engine==.

papers.title: Qdrant 1.20 - Full-Text Search Improvements
papers.summary: Ranking keyword search results with BM25 in Qdrant used to mean turning every document and query into a sparse vector and tracking the average document length yourself, which drifts as data changes. Qdrant 1.20 computes BM25 directly on the full-text index: ==all statistics come from the data automatically, with no vectors to generate==. Parameters can be tuned per query, and it combines with vector search in hybrid queries. The release also adds a code tokenizer, so getUserName and get_user_name match each other, and a 16-bit TurboQuant vector format that halves storage versus the default 32-bit floats, with recall nearly unchanged on 12 datasets.

papers.title: BiLoCo: Binary Low-Rank Corrections for Post-Training Quantization
papers.authors: David Jin, Beshr IslamBouli, Tarushii Goel, Han Guo, Yoon Kim
papers.summary: Quantizing a trained LLM straight to FP4 lets Blackwell GPUs use native FP4 matrix multiplies, but accuracy drops noticeably. The common fix, SVDQuant, stores an extra BF16 low-rank correction, which costs storage and competes with the main computation for the same tensor cores. This paper from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology proposes BiLoCo (binary low-rank correction). Every vector in the correction is replaced by entries of plus or minus one, so ==the correction needs only additions and subtractions and runs on idle CUDA cores alongside the matrix multiply==. The same storage holds 16 times the rank with equal or better perplexity, and at batch size 1 the whole kernel is only 6% to 11% slower than plain FP4.

papers.title: GS-MoE: Training-Free MoE Compression via Groupwise Subspace Sharing and Pruning
papers.authors: Carson Cary, Yukai Jin, Yihao Huang, Zhankai Ye, Fangyi Li, Ting Hua, Xin Liu, Shangqian Gao
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per token, so compute is cheap, but every expert's parameters must stay in GPU memory, and memory is usually the first thing that blocks deployment. This paper proposes GS-MoE, which needs no retraining and compresses experts along two axes at once. First, similar experts are grouped, and ==each group shares one input and one output projection while each expert keeps only a small private matrix==. Second, intermediate neurons inside each expert that other neurons can stand in for are removed. On DeepSeek-MoE-16B with 60% of parameters removed, average accuracy on reasoning tasks stays at about 90% of the original model, versus 73% for the baseline D2-MoE.

papers.title: HyScale: Scaling Long-Context Training for Learned Sparse Attention
papers.authors: Yangsheng Deng, Xinjing Huang, Yulong Wang, Yunzhuo Liu, Jun Hu, Shuyong Tang, Junchi Zeng, Mingji Han, Ray Ying, Key Zh...
papers.summary: Learned sparse attention lets each query read only the k most relevant earlier tokens and is a popular architecture for million-token contexts. But the selection step that picks those k tokens scores every earlier token, and in training it becomes the bottleneck, taking nearly half of each step on long sequences in Megatron-LM. HyScale's key observation is that ==selection outputs only a set of indices, so there is no need to store a full score table or to select again during recomputation==. It finds the exact top k on the fly and reuses the forward-pass indices during recomputation. Training million-token sequences on 512 H20 GPUs, it runs 2.07x faster end to end than Megatron-LM.

papers.title: KnitTrans: Coordinated Trajectory Transfer for Effective and Efficient LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Bangjun Xiao, Chiheng Lou, Xiaodong Ji, Xiangwei Deng, Yikai Zhao, Gang Huang, Hailin Zhang
papers.summary: When LLM reinforcement learning runs generation and training on separate machines, finished trajectories often wait until a whole batch is complete before training, so the trained model drifts further from the version that generated them. Trajectory data is large, and mismatches between how it is moved and how training reads it cause repeated transfers and idle waiting. KnitTrans ==admits finished trajectories into early mini-batches==. A full batch must mix data sources at set ratios, so each admission is checked to leave enough room to fill every source's share. It moves data on demand in the order training consumes it, Several trajectories from the same prompt share its images and other multimodal inputs, so each input is encoded once per mini-batch and reused across them. The version gap drops by up to 93%, and on multimodal workloads transfer plus training is up to 5.8 times faster.

papers.title: NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Nilesh Prasad Pandey, Jangseon Park, Jason Kong, Onat Gungor, Tajana Rosing
papers.summary: In LLM reinforcement learning post-training, generating answers often takes over 70% of training time. This paper notices that the answers a prompt received in recent training rounds closely resemble what it will produce now, so they make good drafts. NgramRL ==builds an n-gram draft table for each prompt from only its own recent answers==. During generation, the last few tokens of the current answer are looked up in the table, what followed them becomes the draft, and the large model verifies several tokens at once. It needs no extra draft model and no GPU memory, and the output distribution stays the same. On reasoning and structured-generation tasks with a warm cache, each forward pass of the large model confirms 3.6 to 7.8 tokens, up to twice as many as SuffixDecoding, a similar method that drafts from a suffix tree over global past answers.

papers.title: OXE-AugE: A Large-Scale Robot Augmentation of OXE for Scaling Cross-Embodiment Policy Learning
papers.authors: Guanhua Ji, Harsha Polavaram, Lawrence Yunliang Chen, Sandeep Bajamahal, Zehan Ma, Simeon Adebola, Chenfeng Xu, Ken Gold...
papers.summary: Generalist robot policies must control many arm and gripper combinations, but recollecting data and retraining for each new robot is too costly. The widely used Open X-Embodiment dataset gathers over sixty robot datasets yet is badly imbalanced: the top four robot types make up over 85% of its real data. This paper builds an augmentation toolkit that extends existing demonstrations to nine other arm and gripper combinations, yielding OXE-AugE with 4.4 million trajectories, more than three times the original. The abstract gives the scale and findings but not how actions are converted to the new robots. Experiments show ==diverse robot augmentation helps not only the augmented robots== but also unseen robots and the original robots under distribution shift.

papers.title: Coupling Execution Horizon and Sampling Depth in Flow-Matching VLA Policies
papers.authors: Jiabing Yang, Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Chenhang Cui, Tao Yu, Zichen Wen, Wen Ye, Bowen Fang...
papers.summary: In flow-matching vision-language-action models, solver steps and execution horizon turn out to be coupled, and the best setting can reverse. These models start from random noise and use a numerical solver to push it step by step into a smooth action chunk. Deployment usually tunes the two separately: the horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver steps stay high for accuracy. Under frequent replanning, fewer solver steps do hurt, but ==when a long stretch of actions runs open loop, fewer solver steps actually help==, because coarse integration keeps actions closer to the mean trajectory and limits compounding drift. Executing 5 actions at a time, 10 solver steps win. Executing 20 at a time, 2 solver steps win. The pattern holds across benchmarks and real robots, cutting latency and raising success without training.

papers.title: FLORA: An Open Model Suite for Scaling Robotics Data Engines
papers.authors: Sicong Leng, Yunze Man, Zhiqi Li, Jing Wang, Yuhe Zhang, Ryan Punamiya, Siddharth Patki, Kaiyuan Zheng, Zi-ang Cao, Zhid...
papers.summary: Training robot foundation models takes huge amounts of labels: deployments need task-success judgments, reinforcement-learning post-training needs per-step process scores, and pretraining needs timestamped captions to filter data. NVIDIA has open-sourced Flora, the data engine used to train GR00T, where ==one model produces all three kinds of labels==. It sets the best scores on public captioning and reward benchmarks and matches GPT-6 Astra on internal tests. It is roughly 125 times cheaper and labels 200,000 hours of data a day on 512 GB300s.

papers.title: DiscoDemo: Discovering Efficient and Diverse Robot Demonstrations for Imitation Learning
papers.authors: Minho Park, Kinam Kim, Donghu Kim, Byungkun Lee, Dongyoon Hwang, Yongjae Shin, Junha Hyung, Hojoon Lee, Jaegul Choo
papers.summary: Imitation learning depends heavily on how widely its demonstrations cover the task, but collecting diverse successful demonstrations is expensive. This paper ==uses reinforcement learning as a data generator rather than a deployable controller==. DiscoDemo trains a generator where each latent code yields a different way to solve the task; training starts from states near the goal and gradually backs off. A diversity reward grows as the states visited under different latent codes lie farther apart in a learned representation, and it is given only to trajectories that complete the task. The generator's trajectories are filtered: failures are dropped, then any with unwanted robot-scene contact or excessive insertion force; the rest become a static dataset for a downstream visuomotor policy. Across four manipulation tasks, average downstream success versus the strongest baseline rises from 40% to 62% in simulation. On the real robot it rises from 39% to 78%.

papers.title: BitVLA: 1-bit Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotics Manipulation
papers.authors: Hongyu Wang, Chuyan Xiong, Ruiping Wang, Xilin CHEN
papers.summary: Vision-language-action models are too large for the edge devices robots carry. Rather than compressing after training, BitVLA uses extreme low-bit weights from the start: every parameter is one of minus one, zero or one, about 1.58 bits, conventionally called a 1-bit model, built on the open BitNet LLM. The vision encoder's weights are quantized to the same three values, and training pulls its image representations toward those of the original full-precision encoder. ==It matches the full-precision OpenVLA-OFT baseline== while cutting model memory by 11 times and end-to-end latency by 4.4 times.

papers.title: No Eyes, No Problem: What Does Touch Contribute to Blind Baoding Ball Manipulation?
papers.authors: Ayush Deshmukh, Nalin Agarwal, Elle Miller, Sethu Vijayakumar
papers.summary: People can spin Baoding balls in one palm without looking, but robots struggle to manipulate for long by touch alone. Blind policies can be trained in simulation, yet on a real dexterous hand contacts change constantly, tactile signals drift with motion, and simulated dynamics differ from reality. This paper uses only joint sensing and on-off tactile signals on a Shadow dexterous hand. In simulation it reproduces the real tactile sensor layout and the tendon-driven coupling of finger joints. It calibrates the on-off threshold of each tactile sensor separately, and adds two new randomizations: random limits on how fast actions can change, and randomly stuck tactile sensors. ==The policy transfers zero-shot to the real hand==, completing 225 consecutive half-turns in one continuous trial with no vision or object position.

papers.title: RealDexUMI: A Wearable Universal Manipulation Interface for Dexterous Robot Learning
papers.authors: Chaoyi Xu, Yixuan Jiang, Jiahui Huan, Yuhui Fu, Hao Yu Zhou, Weitian Yuan, Jiayi Yu, Wanpeng Zhang, Haoqi Yuan, Zongqing...
papers.summary: Dexterous hand demonstrations must keep fine hand-object contact while staying executable at deployment. Existing pipelines either lose fine motions when converting human hand movement to robot hand movement, or rely on costly, unintuitive robot-specific teleoperation rigs. RealDexUMI is a wearable collection device that uses the same dexterous hand module for collection and deployment, with in-hand cameras and fingertip touch sensors. A palm-side glove whose joints mirror the robot hand one to one, so bending a finger joint bends the matching robot joint with no motion conversion. ==Views, touch and actions match exactly between collection and deployment==. Across eight real-robot tasks, average success is 88.75%, and policies transfer across three robots.

papers.title: Regularised RL improves sim-to-real transfer
papers.authors: Danilo Vucetic, Mohamad H. Danesh, Florence Clerc, Hsiu-Chin Lin, Jonathan Tremblay
papers.summary: In theory, regularized reinforcement learning has provable robustness and should ease moving policies from simulation to real robots, yet pipelines still default to the weakly regularized PPO. This paper systematically compares common algorithms on sim-to-real transfer and derives a new one, SMM-AC. Instead of taking the maximum over action values when estimating the next state's value, it uses a smooth maximum: multiply the action values by a parameter ω, exponentiate, average, take the log and divide by ω. A large ω approaches the maximum and ω near 0 approaches the average; this kind of value function is proven robust to a wider set of perturbations. ==It matches the widely used RL algorithm SAC in MuJoCo simulation and earns higher returns on real robots==, staying steadier under perturbations to observations, environment and dynamics. The conclusion: regularization does narrow the sim-to-real gap.

papers.title: Training in Deployment: Human-in-the-loop Online Post-Training for Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Chun Gu, Xiaofei Wei, Yiming Chen, Bozhou Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
papers.summary: When large robot foundation models are adapted to new tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations, the data rarely covers the hard states of deployment, such as contact, recovery from mistakes and precise alignment. TIDE puts robot execution, human takeover, learning and policy updates into one deployment session. The system records whether each action chunk came from the human or the policy, and training feeds that source label to the model as an extra input. When the robot runs on its own, the label is fixed to the human source, so the policy acts the way human takeovers did. ==No value function, reward model or action scorer is needed==, and updated policies go onto the robot at the end of each episode. On four real bimanual tasks, task progress and full completion beat both the starting policy and extra offline demonstrations, and the share of human takeovers falls.

papers.title: Revisiting Temporal Regularization for Smooth Control in Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: SungJae Ahn, Jeong Woon Lee, Kyoleen Kwak, Hyoseok Hwang
papers.summary: Robot policies trained with reinforcement learning often jitter between actions, which wears out motors on real hardware. Existing methods directly limit how much actions change when the input state changes slightly, but these broad constraints hurt task performance as smoothing grows. Penalizing only the difference between consecutive actions was thought unable to handle observation noise. This paper proves that when several current states lead to the same next state, the consecutive-step penalty also shrinks the action differences between them. That amounts to smoothing across nearby states, and experiments show the policy becomes steadier under observation noise. ==CATS uses only the consecutive-step penalty and ramps its weight up linearly from zero==, letting the policy learn to earn reward before it gradually smooths. In simulation and on real robots, action oscillation drops sharply with little loss in task performance.
